title: The biggest battleship ever
pull: Nine guns no warship ever matched
specNote: Main guns: Wikipedia (Yamato), NHHC Online Library page, Japan Tourism Agency text on the Yamato Museum, Navypedia. Length 263 m overall: Wikipedia, Navypedia, and the Yamato Museum's one tenth scale model of 26.3 m (Japan Tourism Agency). Full load: NHHC says over 72,800 tons, Navypedia 72,810 t, Wikipedia 71,659 t; they differ, so the row only claims what all agree on, over 70,000 tons. Standard displacement left out (NHHC about 65,000, Wikipedia 65,027 normal, Navypedia 63,200). Armor belt 410 mm: Wikipedia, Navypedia. Top speed 27 knots: Wikipedia, Navypedia. Peacetime complement left out (sources give 2,500, 2,767, 3,233); 3,332 aboard at the sinking is given by both the Japan Tourism Agency text and Wikipedia.

facts.text: Yamato was laid down at the Kure Naval Arsenal on 4 November 1937, launched on 8 August 1940, and commissioned on 16 December 1941, just over a week after Pearl Harbor.
She carried nine 46 cm (18.1 inch) guns in three triple turrets, the largest guns ever mounted on a warship.
Each of her armor piercing shells weighed about 1,460 kg (3,200 pounds).
She was built in extreme secrecy. Part of the dry dock at Kure was roofed over to hide her from view.
This photo shows her running full power trials on 30 October 1941. US occupation authorities seized it in Japan after the war.
She was 263 m (863 ft) long, with a main armor belt 410 mm (16.1 inches) thick, and could make 27 knots.
She and her sister ship Musashi were the heaviest and most powerfully armed battleships ever built.
On 7 April 1945, sailing on a one way mission toward Okinawa, she was sunk south of Kyushu by American carrier planes. Of the 3,332 men aboard, only a few hundred survived.
Her wreck was found in 1982 and confirmed as Yamato in 1985. A one tenth scale model of her stands in the Yamato Museum at Kure today.

declassified.fact: To hide how big the guns really were, the Japanese Navy officially called them 40 cm guns. The secret held: US intelligence was still listing Yamato's main guns as 16 inch as late as July 1945, three months after she sank.

notes: Evergreen bank card. The date is the photo's date (30 October 1941, full power trials), confirmed on the Commons file page and on the NHHC Online Library page for 80-G-704702. Not a repeat: no posted card is on Yamato (she appears only inside the Samar card, 1944-10-25). Sinking losses differ by source (about 3,055 to 3,063 dead, roughly 270 survivors), so facts say only 'a few hundred survived'. The NHHC H-Gram on Ten-ichi-go (history.navy.mil/about-us/leadership/director/directors-corner/h-grams/h-gram-044/h-044-3.html) returned 503 during research; worth adding as a source if it loads later. The caption should not claim a standard displacement figure (sources split 63,200 to 65,027 t).
